title: Static electricity
ks3: Electricity and electromagnetism: static charge, electrons, attraction and repulsion, electric fields
intro: Rub a balloon on your hair and it sticks to the wall. Practise charges, moving electrons, attraction and repulsion, sparks and lightning.
description: Free KS3 Physics static electricity questions with answers: positive and negative charge, electrons, attraction and repulsion, electric fields, sparks and lightning. Marked instantly, for Year 7, 8 and 9 (ages 9 to 14).

questions.q: You rub a balloon on your jumper. What happens to the balloon?
questions.hint: Rubbing two materials together moves tiny charged particles.
questions.explain: Rubbing moves electrons from one material to the other, so the balloon becomes electrically charged.

questions.q: Two objects have the same type of charge. What happens when they are brought close together?
questions.hint: Like charges…
questions.explain: Like charges repel: two positives push apart, and so do two negatives.

questions.q: A positively charged object is brought near a negatively charged object. What happens?
questions.hint: Opposite charges…
questions.explain: Opposite charges attract, so the objects pull towards each other.

questions.q: What type of charge does an electron have?
questions.hint: Electrons are the particles that move when things become charged.
questions.explain: Electrons are negatively charged. Protons are positive and neutrons have no charge.

questions.q: An object has no overall charge (it is neutral). What does that mean?
options: It has equal amounts of positive and negative charge
It has no electrons at all
questions.hint: Every atom has both kinds of charge.
questions.explain: A neutral object has the same amount of positive charge (protons) as negative charge (electrons), so they cancel out.

questions.q: Two balloons are both rubbed on the same jumper and hung side by side. What happens?
questions.hint: Both balloons get the same type of charge.
questions.explain: Both balloons pick up the same type of charge, and like charges repel, so they push apart.

questions.q: Which is easiest to charge up by rubbing it with a cloth?
options: A metal spoon held in your hand
A copper wire held in your hand
A steel key held in your hand
questions.hint: In which material does the charge stay put?
questions.explain: Plastic is an insulator, so the charge stays where it was rubbed on. In a metal held in your hand, the charge flows away through the metal and through you.

questions.q: A balloon is rubbed on hair. Which particles move from one material to the other?
questions.hint: These are the tiny particles on the outside of atoms.
questions.explain: Only electrons move. Protons are held tightly in the centre of each atom and can't move off.

questions.q: A balloon gains electrons. What charge does it have now?
questions.hint: Electrons are negative.
questions.explain: It has gained extra negative electrons, so it is negatively charged.

questions.q: A balloon is rubbed on someone's hair, and the hair loses electrons. What charge does the hair have now?
questions.hint: It now has more protons than electrons.
questions.explain: Losing negative electrons leaves more positive charge than negative, so the hair is positively charged. That is why it is attracted to the balloon.

questions.q: A polythene rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes negatively charged. What happened?
options: Electrons moved from the cloth onto the rod
Electrons moved from the rod onto the cloth
Protons moved from the cloth onto the rod
questions.hint: Negative means extra electrons.
questions.explain: Electrons moved from the cloth onto the rod. The rod now has more electrons than protons, so it is negative.

questions.q: When a rod is rubbed with a cloth, the rod gains 5000 electrons. How many electrons has the cloth lost?
questions.hint: Charge is not made or destroyed; it just moves.
questions.explain: The electrons on the rod all came from the cloth, so the cloth lost 5000 electrons. The rod is now negative and the cloth positive, by the same amount.

questions.q: An acrylic (Perspex) rod is rubbed with a cloth and becomes positively charged. What happened?
options: Electrons moved from the rod onto the cloth
Protons moved from the cloth onto the rod
Electrons moved from the cloth onto the rod
questions.hint: Only one type of particle can move when things are rubbed.
questions.explain: Only electrons move. The rod lost electrons to the cloth, so it now has more protons than electrons and is positive. The protons never moved.

questions.q: What do we call the region around a charged object where it can push or pull other charges?
questions.hint: Charged objects can act on each other without touching.
questions.explain: A charged object has an electric field around it. Other charges inside the field feel a force.

questions.q: What is lightning?
options: A huge spark caused by charge building up in clouds
questions.hint: Think of a tiny spark from a door handle, but much bigger.
questions.explain: Charge builds up in storm clouds. When there is enough, it jumps to the ground (or to another cloud) as a giant spark: lightning.

questions.q: A charged balloon sticks to a wall that is not charged. Why?
options: The balloon pulls the opposite charges in the wall closer, so they attract
Gravity pulls it to the wall
questions.hint: The balloon's charge affects the electrons in the wall's surface.
questions.explain: The negative balloon pushes electrons in the wall's surface away, leaving the surface slightly positive. Opposite charges attract, so the balloon sticks.

questions.q: You walk across a carpet, touch a metal door handle and feel a small shock. Why?
options: Charge built up on you flows away through the metal
The handle has a battery in it
questions.hint: Metal is a conductor.
questions.explain: Walking on the carpet charges you up. Metal is a conductor, so when you touch it the charge suddenly flows away, giving a tiny spark.

questions.q: A charged plastic rod is held near tiny pieces of paper. What happens?
options: The paper is attracted to the rod
questions.hint: It is like the balloon and the wall.
questions.explain: The rod's charge pulls opposite charges in the paper towards it, so the light pieces of paper jump up to the rod.

questions.q: Which of these is caused by static electricity?
options: A jumper crackling as you pull it over your head
A magnet sticking to the fridge
questions.hint: Listen for tiny sparks.
questions.explain: Pulling off a jumper rubs it against your hair and clothes, so charge builds up. The crackles are tiny sparks as the charge jumps.

questions.q: In a thunderstorm, what is lightning most likely to strike?
options: A tall object, like a tree standing on its own
A low hollow in the ground
A person lying under a bridge
questions.hint: The charge jumps the shortest way to the ground.
questions.explain: Lightning usually strikes the tallest thing around, because that gives the charge the shortest path to the ground. That is why you should not shelter under a lone tree in a storm.

questions.q: You touch a Van de Graaff generator and your hair stands on end. Why?
options: Each hair gets the same charge, so the hairs repel each other
The hairs get the opposite charge to each other
The generator blows air at you
questions.hint: Like charges…
questions.explain: Charge spreads over you and onto every hair. All the hairs have the same type of charge, so they repel each other and stand apart.

questions.q: A charged balloon is moved further away from some tiny pieces of paper. What happens to the force on the paper?
questions.hint: The electric field gets weaker as you go further from the charge.
questions.explain: The electric field around a charged object is strongest close to it and weaker further away, so the pull on the paper gets weaker.

questions.q: When a plane is refuelled, a metal wire connects it to the ground (it is "earthed"). Why?
options: So charge can flow away safely instead of making a spark that could light the fuel
To make the fuel flow faster
To stop the plane rolling away
To charge up the plane's battery
questions.hint: Fuel rubbing through the pipe can build up charge.
questions.explain: Fuel rubbing through the pipe can charge things up. The earthing wire is a conductor, so charge flows away to the ground and can't build up into a dangerous spark near the fuel.

questions.q: A tall building has a thick copper strip running from its roof down into the ground (a lightning conductor). How does it protect the building?
options: If lightning strikes, the charge flows through the copper to the ground instead of through the building
It pushes lightning away from the building
It stores the charge for later
questions.hint: Copper is an excellent conductor.
questions.explain: Copper is a very good conductor, so it gives the lightning's charge an easy path to the ground. The charge flows through the strip and not through the walls.
